The claim in one sentence. fr:title.text: The category ChuG of grammar Chu pairs

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The category ChuG of grammar Chu pairs

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Objects. A Chu pair is (A^+, A^-, \epsilon _A) where A^\pm : \mathbf {Gr} and \epsilon _A : A^+ \mathrel {\And } A^- \vdash \bot is consistency: pointwise, no string carries both a parse and a refutation. The pairing is over \mathrel {\And } (Cartesian), not \otimes — the \otimes -pairing A^+ \otimes A^- \vdash \bot degenerates, forcing one coordinate empty, because concatenation is total in the free monoid (see sss-00BQ).

Morphisms. (A^+, A^-) \to (B^+, B^-) is a pair f^+ : A^+ \vdash B^+ and f^- : B^- \vdash A^- — covariant on parses, contravariant on refutations. The usual Chu compatibility square asks that two composites A^+ \mathrel {\And } B^- \vdash \bot agree; since \bot is the empty grammar, terms into \bot are unique (functions into the empty type form a proposition), so compatibility is automatic. ChuG morphisms are just pairs — no side condition to verify in Agda.

Structure. Since (\mathbf {Gr}, \mathrel {\And }, \top ) is Cartesian closed (function grammar \Rightarrow ), the standard Chu recipe makes ChuG symmetric *-autonomous: dual (A^+, A^-)^* = (A^-, A^+), tensor (A^+ \mathrel {\And } B^+,\; (A^+ \Rightarrow B^-) \mathrel {\And } (B^+ \Rightarrow A^-)), internal hom ((A^+ \Rightarrow B^+) \mathrel {\And } (B^- \Rightarrow A^-),\; A^+ \mathrel {\And } B^-). No Barr-style non-commutative machinery is needed: the Lambek \otimes never enters the Chu structure; it appears only inside the coordinates, lifted pairwise per the connective table.

Parsers. A Parser for A in the sense of the paper is a ChuG object (A, A_\neg ) together with a totality witness \StringGram \vdash A \oplus A_\neg . Consistency is the Chu condition; totality is the extra, parser-specific demand (sss-00BQ).

fr:title.text: Chu interpretation of every grammar type former

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Chu interpretation of every grammar type former

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Each type former of the dependent Lambek DSL lifts to ChuG by pairing positive evidence with its pointwise De Morgan dual. Consistency of every row is structural — checked once per connective, inherited by every grammar built from the table. Extends the core table of sss-00BQ to the full DSL.
\mathsf {NES}(w) = (w \neq \varepsilon ); \neg \mathsf {lit}(c) is "any string other than the one-character string c". Disjointness of each atom pair is immediate.
Additives — evidence forks, refutation intersects (and dually):
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: (A^+,A^-) \mathrel {\And } (B^+,B^-) = (A^+ \mathrel {\And } B^+,\; A^- \oplus B^-) \qquad (A^+,A^-) \oplus (B^+,B^-) = (A^+ \oplus B^+,\; A^- \mathrel {\And } B^-)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The indexed versions lift the same way: a product over x : X pairs with a coproduct over x : X of the refutations, and dually. Caveat: the DSL's indexed coproduct \oplus ^d carries an \mathsf {isSet}\,X requirement while \mathrel {\And }^d does not, so the lift of \mathrel {\And }^d_{x : X} demands \mathsf {isSet}\,X — the refutation side is where the h-level cost lands.
Multiplicatives — a refutation of a concatenation refutes some factor of every split:
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: (A^+,A^-) \otimes (B^+,B^-) = (A^+ \otimes B^+,\; A^- \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} B^-) \qquad (A \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} B)(w) = \forall \, w_1 w_2 = w.\; A(w_1) \oplus B(w_2)
fr:mainmatter.html:p: with \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} lifting dually (\mathbin {\mathsf {par}} on top, \otimes below). Units: \varepsilon for \otimes , \mathsf {NES} for \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}.

Residuals. A refutation of A \multimap B is a witness: some A-context in which the result fails. Writing (A \backslash _\exists B)(w) = \exists u.\, A(u) \times B(uw) for the existential left quotient:

Consistency: applying a parse of A^+ \multimap B^+ to the witness's context u yields uw \in B^+ \mathrel {\And } B^-, contradiction. The left residual mirrors this with the quotient on the other side. The quantifier over u is internalisable by the same sum-encoding pattern as the disjunctive \sqrt {} (a \oplus ^d over \lceil u \rceil -representables), which is where \mathsf {isSet}\,\StringGram enters.
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: \neg (A^+, A^-) = (A^-, A^+) \qquad \mu X.\, F \mapsto {\mathopen {}\left (\mu X^+.\, F^+,\; \nu X^-.\, F^-\right )\mathclose {}}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Negation is coordinate flip — PEG negative lookahead as a denotation. The fixed-point row is the reduct; why it is well-defined and solvable is sss-00EU; when the negative \nu is reachable inductively is sss-00EV. The later modality \rhd lifts componentwise through its indexed-product presentation, with the disjunctive \sqrt {} encoding already carrying its own negative summand.

fr:title.text: What adding par costs: proof relevance, lax laws, splittings

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What adding par costs: proof relevance, lax laws, splittings

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The connective \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}, (A \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} B)(w) = \forall \, w_1 w_2 = w.\; A(w_1) \oplus B(w_2), is the one genuinely new ingredient the reduct demands, and it carries three real costs. All are confined to the middle block of the table — the Chu structure over \mathrel {\And } is untouched.

1. Never a language. The disjuncts sit at different substrings, hence are not exclusive: a \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}-inhabitant is a choice function over splits, and \mathsf {isLang} fails on the negative side even for language coordinates. Decide once: truncate the refutation coordinate (clean laws, opaque failures) or keep proof-relevant refutations (error content, bigger types).

2. Monoidal laws only on the decidable fragment. Associativity needs A(u) \oplus \forall s.\, B \oplus C from \forall s.\, A(u) \oplus B \oplus C — commuting \forall past \oplus , constructively valid only when A(u) is decidable. The \mathsf {NES} unit law is a retraction, not an iso (rebuilt choice functions normalise the disjunct choices). So the lifted Lambek tensor on Chu pairs is monoidal-up-to-logical-equivalence globally, and monoidal-up-to-iso exactly on the total/decidable fragment — the combinator laws hold where parsers exist, gated by dec-Start once again.

3. Quantifying over splittings is the historical perf killer. Path-valued Splittings under hcomp caused the witness-parse blowup; a \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}-refutation is a function over all splits, and Dyck's F^- nests a 4-way one. Implementation must be Eq-world (SplittingEq) from day one. Tested 2026-07-15 (Examples/ParTest.agda, green): the derived \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} DOES compute — refutation witnesses for lit a ⊗ lit b and one Kleene-star unrolling normalise by Eq.refl when interrogated at concrete splits, and the consistency direction (no refutation of members) is provable pointwise. The default \otimes being AsEquality (Eq-world splittings) is what makes this work.

Design note: two pars, not one. \mathsf {NES} must not be baked into \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}'s split quantifier: the proper-split par is unitless (its right part never covers the whole index — the same reason \rhd has no counit), while \mathsf {NES} is a lax unit for the full \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}, with embedding by external case on the \mathrel {\And }^d index — no decidability needed. Instead define both: the semantic \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} (all splits, correct De Morgan complements for nullable factors) and the guarded core \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}^\circ (both parts nonempty, hence FactorsThroughLater by construction), bridged by nullability: when both operands cover \varepsilon , the boundary splits are discharged and \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}^\circ recovers \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}. The F^--contractivity lemma becomes structural for reducts built with \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}^\circ .

Spurious worry: a new primitive. \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} is derivable — an indexed product over context pairs localised by \lceil \cdot \rceil -representables, the same pattern as \sqrt {}-string and \rhd . No new SPFunctor code, no positivity extension; the syntactic reduct emits the derived form. (X^- sits in the split-function's codomain — a positive position — so even a first-class code would be positivity-fine.)

fr:title.text: Why the complement grammar is solvable: the reduct

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why the complement grammar is solvable: the reduct

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Given a recursive grammar A = \mu X.\, F(X) written in the connectives of the table, the complement is computed, not chosen: walk F syntactically to get F(X^+, X^-) = (F^+, F^-), then take
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: (A^+, A^-) = {\mathopen {}\left (\mu X^+.\, F^+(X^+, Y^-),\; \nu X^-.\, F^-(Y^+, X^-)\right )\mathclose {}}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: closed by the outer \mu ^i Y when F mentions negation. When F is negation-free — every DSL SPFunctor code — F^+ depends only on X^+ and F^- only on X^-, so the doubling collapses to two independent fixed points: A^+ is the grammar as written, A^- its complement.

Why consistency survives the fixed point. Each table row preserves pointwise disjointness, but (\mu F^+, \nu F^-) needs its own argument: given a parse (a finite tree in \mu F^+) and a refutation (a possibly infinite tree in \nu F^-) of the same w, unroll both one layer; the one-step consistency of the lifted connectives pushes the contradiction to some child position, at a shorter-or-equal substring, and the parse tree is well-founded, so the descent bottoms out at an atom pair — which is disjoint by construction. Finiteness of the positive side is what makes the bilateral pair consistent; no condition on the refutation side is needed.

Why totality is the only residual theorem — and must be. The reduct outputs a ChuG pair; a Parser additionally needs \StringGram \vdash A^+ \oplus A^-. This cannot be structural: DSL grammars embed arbitrary propositions (indexed products over any type), so uniform totality would decide them. Totality is exactly where language-theoretic content enters: regular, LL(k), DCFL — or, for any CNF-presentable CFG, the CYK completeness route: the parse-forest parser is complete, so an empty forest is itself the refutation, and totality falls out of forest decidability. The reduct reduces "build a verified total parser" to "prove this one disjunction".

Worked example. sss-00BQ runs Dyck through the table: the positive side is Dyck unchanged; the negative side is \mathsf {NES} \mathrel {\And } (\neg \mathsf {lit}(a) \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} X^- \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} \neg \mathsf {lit}(b) \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} X^-), with sanity checks for a, ab, b.

fr:title.text: Parsing with derivatives for a locally contractive family of grammars

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Parsing with derivatives for a locally contractive family of grammars

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Goal. Give a single, generic parser — producing parse trees, not an accept/reject bit — that works for any locally contractive endofunctor F on families of grammars, taking local-contractivity of F as the only hypothesis. In the intrinsic setting a grammar is its family of parse trees: a parse of w in G is an element of ⟦G⟧ w. So the parser must produce inhabitants of ⟦G*⟧ w (a whole forest, for ambiguous G), and the derivative must carry those inhabitants. This is the confluence of the derivative cluster with the local-contractivity / hylomorphism machinery: a recursive grammar family is the unique fixed point of a locally contractive functor, and its parser is the family hylomorphism that transports parse trees through the chain of derivative isomorphisms.

Conventions as in sss-00EZ, but read proof-relevantly: ε is the empty-string grammar, ⊥ the empty grammar, · concatenation, ⊕ alternation, char a a literal, δ c the derivative. Write ν G for the ε-part grammar of G — the subgrammar carrying exactly G's empty-string parses, (ν G) ε = G ε and ⊥ elsewhere. This is a grammar (it holds parse trees), not a Boolean; the recognizer's ν? is only its collapse to inhabited-or-not.

fr:title.text: Setup: a family of grammars as the fixed point of a contractive functor

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Setup: a family of grammars as the fixed point of a contractive functor

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Grammars are presheaves over (\stringg , \sqsubseteq ), \sqsubseteq the suffix order. A family of grammars is G : I \to \mathbf {Gr} for an index type I (the nonterminals / reachable derivative states). The later modality \rhd is front-consuming, (\rhd G)\,w = \prod _{u \sqsubset w} G\,u.

A functor F : \mathbf {Gr}^I \to \mathbf {Gr}^I is locally contractive when it factors through \rhd fibrewise — F(G)_i\,w depends on G only at proper suffixes of w. By the combinator calculus this is automatic when F is built from constants, the one-step guards char a · (−), and ⊕ / · / ⊗ positionwise: the grammar functor language, i.e. the string-ranked containers. Local contractivity gives a unique fixed point G^\ast = \mu F \cong F(G^\ast ) (Löb / Banach) — the recursive grammar family we parse. "F locally contractive" replaces every earlier guardedness device.

fr:title.text: Step 1 — the derivative is a proof-relevant iso; parsing transports trees

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Step 1 — the derivative is a proof-relevant iso; parsing transports trees

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Every grammar decomposes by first character, as a grammar isomorphism that carries parse trees:
G ≅ ν G ⊕ ⊕[c] char c · δ c G.
A parse of ε lands in ν G; a parse of c ∷ w splits as "the character c, then a parse of δ c G on w". The engine of the whole construction is the derivative iso
deriv : char c · G ≅ δ c G , equivalently (δ c G) w ≅ G (c ∷ w) ,
which is proof-relevant both ways: deriv pushes a "c-then-G" tree into a δ c G tree, and deriv⁻¹ recovers it. This is the ⟜-as-derivative content, not a decision.

The guard behaves as the character-indexed \rhd _c of sss-00AC, and the derivative is its force: from the adjunction {\mathopen {}\left (\char c \cdot -\right )\mathclose {}} \dashv \delta c of sss-00EY,

html:p.html:code: δ c (char c · G) = δ c(char c) · G ⊕ ν(char c) · δ c G = ε · G ⊕ ⊥ = G

fr:mainmatter.html:p: is the unit iso — differentiating past the guard by its own character returns the guarded grammar, with its parse tree intact (the leading c stripped). δ c' (char c · G) = ⊥ for c' ≠ c.

fr:title.text: Step 2 — functor-level keystone: local contractivity makes δ total

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Step 2 — functor-level keystone: local contractivity makes δ total

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Lemma. If F is locally contractive then, for every family G, δ c (F G) depends on G but not on δ c G.

Proof. Push δ c through F by the (proof-relevant) chain rule δ c (A · B) = δ c A · B ⊕ ν A · δ c B. Every recursive occurrence of G sits under a guard char a · (⋯G⋯) — that is what local contractivity is. The branch that would recurse toward δ c G is ν(char a) · δ c(⋯G⋯), and ν(char a) = ⊥ (a literal has no empty parse) kills it; the other branch keeps (⋯G⋯), hence G, undifferentiated. So δ c(F G) never contains δ c G. ∎

Consequence. On the fixed point δ c G^\ast = δ c(F G^\ast ) is a residual over G^\ast (undifferentiated) and derivatives of the non-recursive parts — computed by one unfolding of F, no circular δ c G^\ast . Hence δ c is total on the whole reachable derivative family, generically, for any locally contractive F. This promotes the sss-00EZ keystone from a syntactic argument to a corollary of local contractivity — and because δ is proof-relevant, it transports parse trees while it goes.

fr:title.text: Step 3 — the parser as a family hylomorphism

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Step 3 — the parser as a family hylomorphism

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The parser produces the parse forest parse G* w : ⟦G*⟧ w by walking the derivative isos down to ε and reshaping back:

html:p.html:code: parse G* ε = the ε-parses of G* ( inhabitants of (ν G*) ε )
parse G* (c ∷ w) = deriv⁻¹ (parse (δ c G*) w)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: where parse (δ c G*) w : (δ c G*) w reshapes along (δ c G*) w ≅ G* (c ∷ w) into a parse of the full string. Nothing here is Boolean: each step transports an actual tree, and the ε-base returns the set of empty-string parse trees (many, for ambiguous G*), so the output is the full parse forest.

This is exactly a HyloFam: the coalgebra unfolds the input against the derivative dynamics δ (the contractive strength, sss-00EP/sss-00EO; the mate G\circ H\circ U is locally contractive), and the algebra folds parse trees back up through deriv⁻¹; the carrier is the parse family ⟦G*⟧. Totality combines (i) each δ c step total (Step 2) with (ii) structural recursion on the input, terminating in |w| steps. The reachable derivative family is infinite for non-regular G^\ast , but a single parse visits only the length-|w| path — the hylo never materialises the state space.

fr:title.text: Step 4 — soundness and completeness are automatic: the parser is an iso

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Step 4 — soundness and completeness are automatic: the parser is an iso

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The whole fold is the composite of proof-relevant derivative isos
⟦G*⟧ w = ⟦G*⟧ (c₁⋯cₙ) ≅ ⟦δ c₁ G*⟧ (c₂⋯cₙ) ≅ ⋯ ≅ ⟦δ_w G*⟧ ε ,

using G* ≅ F G* and the Step-2 identity to compute each step. So parse G* is not a recognizer whose correctness needs proving — it is this bijection computed. Soundness (every produced tree is a genuine parse) and completeness (every genuine parse is produced) hold by construction, because each deriv is an isomorphism; semantic actions ride along the isos untouched. The μ = ν coincidence for the guarded fixed point says G^\ast is at once the initial algebra (parse trees exist inductively) and the final coalgebra (they are exactly the language's parses), so "the parse forest" is unambiguous as an object.

fr:title.text: Worked example: a mutually recursive family

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Worked example: a mutually recursive family

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Take I = \{S, T\} and
F(G)_S = char a · G_T · char b ⊕ ε , F(G)_T = char c · G_S · char d ⊕ ε.
δ a S = ε · (T · char b) ⊕ ⊥ = T · char b , δ c T = S · char d , others ⊥.
Parsing acdb in S descends four derivative isos to an ε-parse and reshapes back to a parse tree:

html:p.html:code: S --a--> T · char b --c--> S · char d · char b --d--> char b --b--> ε

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The ε-parse at the end is the innermost S → ε; deriv⁻¹ applied four times rebuilds
S( a , T( c , S(ε) , d ) , b ) ,
i.e. the actual nested tree, not a yes. No fixed point was solved and only the four states on the path were touched.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Where this lives

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Objects. A Chu pair is (A^+, A^-, \epsilon _A) where A^\pm : \mathbf {Gr} and \epsilon _A : A^+ \mathrel {\And } A^- \vdash \bot is consistency: pointwise, no string carries both a parse and a refutation. fr:title.text: Why the complement grammar is solvable: the reduct

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why the complement grammar is solvable: the reduct

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Given a recursive grammar A = \mu X.\, F(X) written in the connectives of the table, the complement is computed, not chosen: walk F syntactically to get F(X^+, X^-) = (F^+, F^-), then take
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: (A^+, A^-) = {\mathopen {}\left (\mu X^+.\, F^+(X^+, Y^-),\; \nu X^-.\, F^-(Y^+, X^-)\right )\mathclose {}}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: closed by the outer \mu ^i Y when F mentions negation. When F is negation-free — every DSL SPFunctor code — F^+ depends only on X^+ and F^- only on X^-, so the doubling collapses to two independent fixed points: A^+ is the grammar as written, A^- its complement.

Why consistency survives the fixed point. Each table row preserves pointwise disjointness, but (\mu F^+, \nu F^-) needs its own argument: given a parse (a finite tree in \mu F^+) and a refutation (a possibly infinite tree in \nu F^-) of the same w, unroll both one layer; the one-step consistency of the lifted connectives pushes the contradiction to some child position, at a shorter-or-equal substring, and the parse tree is well-founded, so the descent bottoms out at an atom pair — which is disjoint by construction. Finiteness of the positive side is what makes the bilateral pair consistent; no condition on the refutation side is needed.

Why totality is the only residual theorem — and must be. The reduct outputs a ChuG pair; a Parser additionally needs \StringGram \vdash A^+ \oplus A^-. This cannot be structural: DSL grammars embed arbitrary propositions (indexed products over any type), so uniform totality would decide them. Totality is exactly where language-theoretic content enters: regular, LL(k), DCFL — or, for any CNF-presentable CFG, the CYK completeness route: the parse-forest parser is complete, so an empty forest is itself the refutation, and totality falls out of forest decidability. The reduct reduces "build a verified total parser" to "prove this one disjunction".

Worked example. sss-00BQ runs Dyck through the table: the positive side is Dyck unchanged; the negative side is \mathsf {NES} \mathrel {\And } (\neg \mathsf {lit}(a) \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} X^- \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} \neg \mathsf {lit}(b) \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} X^-), with sanity checks for a, ab, b.

fr:title.text: The negative fixed point, μ=ν coincidence, and Löb

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The negative fixed point, μ=ν coincidence, and Löb

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The reduct puts a \nu on the refutation side. Three questions decide whether refutations are computable: does \nu F^- exist, is it inductive, and can refute be built by guarded recursion?
Existence is now library fact: Grammar.Coinductive.Indexed provides \nu , corec, and finality on the box branch — the prerequisite flagged in sss-00BQ is discharged.

The 
u is canonical; \mu is sometimes a bonus. The consistency argument of sss-00EU recurses only along the finite parse tree, so even infinitely deep refutations are sound. And 
u is semantically necessary: for the unguarded A = \mu X.\, X =  ot (the empty grammar), F^- = X^- gives \mu X^-. X^- =  ot — no refutations, totality fails — while 
u X^-. X^- = 	op is the true complement, inhabited everywhere by the constant corec. Initial/final coincidence must therefore be treated as a fragment privilege, never a pipeline assumption.

In the guarded fragment, coincidence upgrades refutations to certificates. For locally contractive functors, initial algebra and final coalgebra coincide; if F^- is locally contractive at the suffix (or span) order, then \nu X^-. F^- = \mu X^-. F^-: refutations are finite, and refute is a fold. This is the reduct's consumer of the CCL coincidence machinery (sss-00EF, items 1 and 6). Outside the fragment, refute is built by corec instead, and totality may still hold coinductively (as in the \mu X. X example: \mathsf {inr} \circ \mathsf {corec}). Negation-containing F (Liar-style, genuine outer \mu ^i) never has a coincidence to hope for.

Caution — guardedness does not transfer for free. Dualising \otimes \mapsto \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} changes where recursion sits: in Dyck's F^- = \mathsf {NES} \mathrel {\And } (\neg \mathsf {lit}(a) \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} X^- \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} \neg \mathsf {lit}(b) \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} X^-), the \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} quantifies over all splits, including degenerate ones that place X^- at the full string (padding other factors with \varepsilon ). So an F^--refutation may choose an unguarded disjunct; productivity is by choice, not by shape. The lemma to prove: if F is Guarded (in the CodeGuarded sense), then F^- is locally contractive — plausibly via \mathsf {NES} forcing progress on the split that matters — but it is a genuine lemma, not an inheritance. sss-00BQ's claim that "the negative recursion is well-founded by string length" is exactly this obligation.

Löb builds refute. Once F^- is locally contractive, refute : \StringGram \vdash A^- \oplus \top -shaped producers arise by lob exactly as parsers do — the a2c (corecursive-algebra) half of the bilateral stack is the formal dual of Theorem 3.7, and the \rhd -guarded fixpoint supplies its productivity. Both halves run off one well-foundedness proof and one shared Brzozowski coalgebra.

Pipeline (updating sss-00BT's bootstrap workflow): write F once; lift to (F^+, F^-); take (\mu F^+, \nu F^-); share one Brzozowski-derivative coalgebra on \StringGram ; parse = unique c2a-morphism into \mu F^+, refute = unique a2c-morphism into \nu F^-; prove totality for the fragment at hand. Ordered choice (A^+ \oplus (A^- \otimes B^+),\; A^- \mathrel {\And } B^-) and negative lookahead (coordinate flip) then give a deterministic complete parser-combinator vocabulary — the Chu route to completeness, complementary to the backtracking parse-forest route.

Implementation order. (1) ChuG record + morphisms (compatibility is free; see sss-00ES) and the atomic + additive rows; (2) multiplicative rows (needs \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} and \mathsf {NES} as library grammars); (3) the code-walking lift on SPFunctor descriptions, following the CodeGuarded pattern; (4) the F Guarded \Rightarrow F^- locally contractive lemma (sss-00EV); (5) Dyck totality as the worked example. Steps 1–3 are library work; 4 is the one open lemma; 5 is the demonstration.

fr:title.text: The bridge

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The bridge

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The Cass–Urbat–Wißmann picture: an intrinsically correct algorithm is the unique c2a-morphism from a recursive coalgebra (C, \gamma : C \to FC) to an algebra (A, \alpha : FA \to A). For a parser, the algebra is \mu F^+ and the coalgebra is the input string with derivative structure. Parse is intrinsically correct because it is unique. This is a purely positive story.
Atkey's reduct is the bilateral generalisation. The doubled fixed point
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: D \;=\; \mu ^i Y.\;{\mathopen {}\left (\mu X^+.\, F^+(X^+, Y^-),\;\nu X^-.\, F^-(Y^+, X^-)\right )\mathclose {}}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: forces a \mu on the positive side and a \nu on the negative side. The two sides have dual recursion principles, which already exist in the literature as the two halves of Capretta–Uustalu– Vene:

html:ul.html:li: Positive. Initial algebra \mu F^+; recursion principle is recursive coalgebra (CUV 2006). Style: catamorphism / fold / well-founded. Computes a parse tree.
Negative. Terminal coalgebra \nu F^-; recursion principle is corecursive algebra (CUV 2009). Style: anamorphism / unfold / productive. Computes a refutation trace.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: So the reduct is a recursive-coalgebra / corecursive-algebra bialgebraic construction, doubly nested: an outer \mu ^i in \mathbf {Chu}^i parameterising an inner \mu on the positive side and an inner \nu on the negative side. Each layer has a known universal property. None of this is new — what is new is that putting them together gives complement grammars under recursion.

fr:title.text: Cass's lever fires twice

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Cass's lever fires twice

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Cass's claim: the inverse of an initial algebra is always a recursive coalgebra, regardless of whether it is the final coalgebra. Apply it twice in the reduct stack:

html:ul.html:li: Inner positive. D^+ = \mu X^+.\, F^+(X^+, Y^-) (with Y^- fixed) is an initial algebra. Its inverse is recursive \Rightarrow structural recursion on parse trees works without step-indexing or guarded modalities.

Outer \mu ^i. The outer fixed point is an initial algebra in \mathbf {Chu}^i. By the same lemma — lifted to \mathbf {Chu}^i, which needs a separate check — its inverse is recursive \Rightarrow recursion on the stage of knowledge Y is well-founded.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Dually, the standard CUV theorem the inverse of a terminal coalgebra is a corecursive algebra fires on the negative side, giving productivity for refutation generation. So the negative half also avoids guarded modalities, again contingent on the lemma transporting to our setting.

fr:title.text: Fit with the derivative-based CFG parser plan

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Fit with the derivative-based CFG parser plan

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Phases 1–6 of sss-00A3 build the positive half: CFGDesc defines F^+; Brzozowski derivatives define an input coalgebra \mathsf {String} \to \hat {F}\, \mathsf {String}; the parser is the unique c2a-morphism into D^+ = \mu F^+.
Adding the Chu partner D^- is the same shape of work, dualised:

html:ol.html:li: Compute F^- from CFGDesc by walking the syntax (this is the GL reduct on the grammar description).
Set D^- = \nu F^-, the terminal coalgebra of refutations.
The refutation function is the unique a2c-morphism out of the same input coalgebra \mathsf {String} \to \hat {F}\, \mathsf {String}, into D^-.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The input coalgebra is shared. Brzozowski's derivative just decomposes the input — it does not commit to a direction. Both the c2a-fold (parse) and the a2c-unfold (refute) consume the same derivative coalgebra. The Chu pair (\mathsf {parse}, \mathsf {refute}) is two morphisms with a common source.

Totality \StringGram \vdash D^+ \oplus D^- is then a theorem about the two morphisms — that they partition input space — not a part of the construction itself. Provable for decidable fragments (LL(k), DCFL like Dyck), not provable in general.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Connecting Atkey on data types with negation to our Parser construction in grammars-and-semantic-actions, with a concrete plan for syntactically deriving the complement of the goal A_\neg from a recursive grammar definition rather than choosing it cleverly by hand.

fr:title.text: Our Parser is a Chu pair plus totality

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Our Parser is a Chu pair plus totality

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In our paper a parser for a grammar A is a choice of a grammar A_\neg together with

The first is exactly the \mathbf {Chu}(\bot ) consistency condition A^+ \times A^- \to \bot . The second is totality (every string is classified), which Atkey does not impose — he allows \mathsf {Liar} \cong (\bot ,\bot ) — but which is the right additional demand for parsers because parsing must decide.

So what we have is the 2-valued, totalising specialisation of Atkey's construction. The Chu structure was already there; we just hadn't named it. A_\neg is positive evidence of failure (typically a rejecting DFA trace), not the function type A \Rightarrow \bot from Grammar/Negation/Base.agda. That matches Atkey: refutations are first-class data, not negated proofs.

Practical consequence: the cleverness we currently spend on choosing A_\neg per grammar is what Atkey's reduct would mechanise. The reduct walks the recursive definition syntactically and computes both A^+ and A^- from the same expression. We never have to invent a refutation grammar; we read it off the structure of the positive grammar.

fr:title.text: Lambek connectives in Chu over Grammar

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Lambek connectives in Chu over Grammar

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Each connective on Grammar lifts to Chu pairs by separating positive evidence from negative evidence:

The first two rows are the Cartesian product and coproduct of \mathbf {Chu}(\mathbf {Gr}, \mathrel {\And }, \bot ) — forced by the construction, with negation flipping coordinates. This block is the symmetric *-autonomous Chu category Atkey works in, transported from (\mathbf {Set}, \times , \emptyset ) to our setting.

The middle two rows lift the Lambek tensor \otimes and its pointwise De Morgan dual (A \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} B)(w) = \forall \text { splits } w_1 w_2 = w.\; A(w_1) \oplus B(w_2) to Chu pairs by symmetric pattern matching: positive on positive, dual on dual. These are not the symmetric Chu tensor — they encode a separate non-commutative Lambek monoidal structure on Chu pairs, which is what actual grammars use.

Unit of \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}. The grammar \mathsf {NES}(w) = (w 
eq \varepsilon ) is a unit for \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}: for w 
eq \varepsilon , every split has either w_1 
eq \varepsilon (making NES hold) or w_1 = \varepsilon (making the A branch fire); for w = \varepsilon , only the trivial split exists and A(\varepsilon ) is required. So the Lambek unit lifts to \varepsilon \mapsto (\varepsilon ,\, \mathsf {NES}).

Caveat — Grammar is not *-autonomous. A^{**} \neq A because A \multimap \bot collapses (the linear function space into \bot kills variation in A). So \mathbin {\mathsf {par}} on Grammar gets a unit but (\otimes , \mathbin {\mathsf {par}}, \varepsilon , \mathsf {NES}) is not a self-dual closed structure on Grammar itself. Duality lives at the Chu level — the Chu-consistency condition A^+ \mathrel {\And } A^- \vdash \bot is what makes the lifted operations well-typed in the first place.

Atomic lifts. A character c lifts to (\mathsf {lit}(c),\, \neg \mathsf {lit}(c)) where \neg \mathsf {lit}(c) is the ordinary grammar "any string distinct from a single character c". The recursion variable X lifts to (X^+, X^-). Pointwise disjointness holds for each lift by construction.

Strictly positive functor separation. A strictly positive recursive grammar F(X) uses only the connectives in the table with X appearing positively, and so lifts to a Chu functor F(X^+, X^-) = (F^+(X^+, X^-),\, F^-(X^+, X^-)) by walking the syntax. When F contains no negation, the lift specialises further — F^+ depends only on X^+ and F^- only on X^- — so the doubled fixed point
fr:mainmatter.fr:tex: D \;=\; \mu ^i Y.\; {\mathopen {}\left (\mu X^+.\, F^+(X^+, Y^-),\;\nu X^-.\, F^-(Y^+, X^-)\right )\mathclose {}}
fr:mainmatter.html:p: collapses to two independent inner fixed points and the outer \mu ^i becomes trivial. For finite-string grammars where the negative recursion is well-founded by string length, the inner \nu agrees with \mu .

fr:title.text: What we need in the codebase

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What we need in the codebase

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Four pieces, in order of independence:

html:ul.html:li: Final coalgebras. The reduct uses \nu on the refutation side, and we currently have only \mu (Grammar.Inductive.Indexed, Kleene star). The user has implemented terminal coalgebras for indexed containers in this codebase before and deleted that work; restoring it is the prerequisite for everything else here. The construction is not research — it is library work.

Chu-over-Grammar as a defined category. A record \mathsf {ChuG} = (A^+ : \mathbf {Gr}) \times (A^- : \mathbf {Gr}) \times (A^+ \mathrel {\And } A^- \vdash \bot ). The pairing uses \mathrel {\And } (Cartesian product on \mathbf {Gr}), not \otimes (Lambek concatenation): A^+ \mathrel {\And } A^- \vdash \bot unfolds to \forall w.\, \neg (A^+(w) \times A^-(w)), the pointwise disjointness condition that already lives in our Parser record. The pairing A^+ \otimes A^- \vdash \bot is a different — and degenerate — condition: it unfolds to \forall w_1\, w_2.\, \neg (A^+(w_1) \times A^-(w_2)), which forces one of A^\pm to be everywhere empty (concatenation is total in the free monoid). So Chu over (\mathrel {\And }, \bot ) is the construction we want; Chu over (\otimes , \bot ) kills all non-trivial pairs. Since \mathrel {\And } is Cartesian, \mathsf {ChuG} is a symmetric *-autonomous category by the standard recipe — no Barr-style non-commutative machinery needed.

Show our Parser factors through Chu. Parser A B should become ChuG (A, B) together with a totality witness \StringGram \vdash A \oplus B. The wk-eqv-parse lemma transports along weak equivalence in the positive coordinate; verify it factors through the Chu morphism structure.

The reduct theorem. A polynomial-functor language for grammars-with-complement, with the doubled-fixed-point initial-algebra theorem proven in our setting. Atkey works in (\mathbf {Set}, \times , \emptyset ); we work in (\mathbf {Gr}, \mathrel {\And }, \bot ). The reduct argument is generic over a Cartesian closed base, and \mathbf {Gr} is Cartesian closed under \mathrel {\And }, so transcription is mostly mechanical once \nu is back in the library. The non-commutative \otimes does not enter the *-autonomous structure of ChuG — it appears only as content inside the polynomial functors F^\pm that describe recursive grammars.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What's in the literature. de Paiva (2018) and de Paiva, Eades & Jiang (2019) construct Dialectica-style models of Lambek directly, using the non-commutative \otimes . Dialectica is a refinement of Chu — it adds a relation between A^+ and A^- rather than a pairing into a fixed dualiser — and they choose to put the non-commutativity in the Chu/Dialectica structure itself. Our choice above is different: we keep the *-autonomous structure symmetric (over \mathrel {\And }) and let the non-commutative \otimes appear inside positive and negative grammars rather than between them. Both choices are defensible; ours is closer to Atkey's Set-based template. Barr (1995) is the relevant reference for the alternative route — Chu over a biclosed non-commutative tensor with two implications. We do not currently need it, but it is what would be required to put \otimes into the Chu structure should that turn out to matter for some application (e.g. a non-commutative Chu where the two implications model directional parsing strategies). Neither de Paiva paper nor the slides develop the formal-language / parser-totality side; that gap is what the synthesis tree and the present tree address.

Decidability/totality is the orthogonal concern. The reduct gives us a Chu pair (D^+, D^-) with consistency for free; whether the resulting (D^+, D^-) is total (i.e. yields a Parser) remains a separate theorem. For Dyck this is just the statement that Dyck is a DCFL, which is true.

fr:title.text: Side benefits of the *-autonomous structure

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Side benefits of the *-autonomous structure

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Once \mathsf {ChuG} is in place we get a *-autonomous category over our grammar SMC for free, with a linear negation (A^+, A^-)^* = (A^-, A^+) and a par. Two things this opens up:

html:ul.html:li: Coinductive parsing. The same \nu that powers the reduct lets us write streaming/online parsers and parsers for non-well-founded languages directly. The user already had ▷-style work in sss-00BE and sss-00B9; reviving final coalgebras dovetails with that.

PEG-style negative lookahead as a primitive grammar. With the reduct in place, a former !A (anything but A) can be a primitive grammar with denotational semantics, instead of an operational hack. This is the application Atkey originally sells the construction on.

fr:title.text: Honest mismatches with Atkey

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Honest mismatches with Atkey

html:ul.html:li: Atkey works in \mathbf {Set} with \times ; we work in \mathbf {Gr} with \mathrel {\And }. Both are Cartesian closed, so the *-autonomous Chu structure transports without extra work. The non-commutative \otimes on \mathbf {Gr} is content inside the recursive functors F^\pm , not part of the Chu structure.

We require totality (string parses as either A^+ or A^-). Atkey does not, and his examples \mathsf {Liar} \cong (\bot ,\bot ) and \mathsf {NoBaseCase} \cong (\bot , \top ) require this slack. Our totalising specialisation forbids them, which is correct for parsers.
No formal-language-theoretic development in the slides — closure, decidability, and grammar-theoretic results are all on us.
